titlePl: Matura PR: Nauka i technika — 180 haseł do gier LingoSpark
titleEn: Matura Extended: Science and technology — 180 terms for LingoSpark games
blurbPl: Dział Nauka i technika na maturę rozszerzoną: badania naukowe, ICT, kosmos, sztuczna inteligencja i zagrożenia cyfrowe. Fiszki ENG–PL.
blurbEn: Extended-level Matura Science and technology vocabulary: research, ICT, space, AI and digital risks. ENG–PL flashcards for LingoSpark games.

items.definitionEn: the science of matter, energy, force and motion
items.example: Physics explains why satellites stay in orbit.

items.definitionEn: the science of substances, their structure and how they react
items.example: Chemistry in the lab requires goggles, not just curiosity.

items.definitionEn: the study of living things at the level of DNA, proteins and cells
items.example: Molecular biology underpins modern genetic tests.

items.definitionEn: the scientific study of stars, planets and other objects in space
items.example: Astronomy is a science; astrology is not.

items.definitionEn: the branch of physics that explains how objects in space behave
items.example: Astrophysics uses both telescopes and computer models.

items.definitionEn: the science of genes, heredity and variation in living things
items.example: Genetics can explain why some diseases run in families.

items.definitionEn: the use of living cells or organisms to make products or solve problems
items.example: Biotechnology produces insulin that used to come only from animals.

items.definitionEn: engineering of materials and devices at an extremely small, atomic scale
items.example: Nanotechnology is used in some medical tests and new materials.

items.definitionEn: the design and use of robots to do tasks
items.example: Robotics in factories has changed the skills employers look for.

items.definitionEn: the scientific study of the brain and nervous system
items.example: Neuroscience is still far from a full map of human memory.

items.definitionEn: the study of microscopic organisms such as bacteria and viruses
items.example: Microbiology showed how quickly a strain can become resistant.

items.definitionEn: the chemistry of processes inside living organisms
items.example: Biochemistry explains how enzymes speed up reactions in cells.

items.definitionEn: the study of computation, algorithms and how computers are designed and used
items.example: Computer science is more than learning to use an office program.

items.definitionEn: the study of the properties and uses of metals, plastics, ceramics and similar substances
items.example: Materials science helped create lighter batteries for electric cars.

items.definitionEn: the physics of the very small, where particles do not behave like everyday objects
items.example: Quantum physics is the basis of some new types of computer.

items.definitionEn: the physics of the nucleus of the atom, including fission and fusion
items.example: Nuclear physics is used in medicine as well as in power stations.

items.definitionEn: the practical use of science to design machines, structures and systems
items.example: Engineering turns a laboratory idea into something that can be built safely.

items.definitionEn: scientific work aimed at solving a practical problem, not only at theory
items.example: Applied science links university labs with industry.

items.definitionEn: the group of sciences that study living organisms, including biology and medicine
items.example: Careers in the life sciences range from lab work to public policy.

items.definitionEn: scientific work based on models and reasoning rather than a new experiment
items.example: Theoretical research can predict a particle years before it is found.

items.definitionEn: a testable idea that an experiment is designed to support or reject
items.example: A hypothesis must be specific enough to be proved wrong.

items.definitionEn: checking a study by other experts before it is published
items.example: Peer review does not make a paper perfect, but it catches many errors.

items.definitionEn: an important discovery or invention that changes what is possible
items.example: The breakthrough in battery chemistry cut charging times in half.

items.definitionEn: the group in a study that does not receive the new treatment, used for comparison
items.example: Without a control group you cannot tell if the drug really worked.

items.definitionEn: a trial in which neither the patient nor the researcher knows who got the real treatment
items.example: A double-blind study reduces bias in both volunteers and doctors.

items.definitionEn: money given to fund a scientific project, usually after a competition
items.example: The research grant will pay for equipment and two years of staff time.

items.definitionEn: a periodical that publishes research papers after expert checks
items.example: A post on social media is not the same as a paper in a scientific journal.

items.definitionEn: a formal mention of another piece of research in a paper
items.example: Every claim in the report needs a scholarly reference, not a vague “scientists say”.

items.definitionEn: the system of methods used in a particular study
items.example: Weak methodology can make even a large study unreliable.

items.definitionEn: to repeat a test to see if the same results appear
items.example: Other labs could not replicate an experiment, so the claim was withdrawn.

items.definitionEn: a statistical link between two things that does not by itself prove cause
items.example: There is a correlation between ice-cream sales and drowning — heat explains both.

items.definitionEn: a relationship in which one thing actually makes another happen
items.example: Journalists often confuse correlation with causation.

items.definitionEn: a measure of whether a result is likely to be a real effect, not chance
items.example: Statistical significance is not the same as a result that matters in real life.

items.definitionEn: the number of people or items included in a study
items.example: A sample size of twelve is too small for a national claim.

items.definitionEn: research done outside the laboratory, in the real environment
items.example: Geologists still need field research, not only satellite photos.

items.definitionEn: the first working model of a new machine or product
items.example: The prototype was ugly, but it proved the idea could fly.

items.definitionEn: a legal right that stops others copying an invention for a limited time
items.example: The company filed a patent before it showed the device at the fair.

items.definitionEn: moving an invention from a laboratory into commercial or public use
items.example: Universities now fight over technology transfer from jointly funded labs.

items.definitionEn: rules that protect people, animals and honesty in scientific work
items.example: Research ethics forbid hiding data that weaken your favourite theory.

items.definitionEn: using animals in experiments, especially to check safety of drugs or products
items.example: Many voters want stricter limits on animal testing.

items.definitionEn: based on systematic research rather than opinion or tradition
items.example: Ministers promised an evidence-based policy on screen use in schools.

items.definitionEn: researchers as a group who share methods, journals and criticism
items.example: The scientific community corrected the error in a later paper.

items.definitionEn: a factor that can change in an experiment and may affect the result
items.example: Change only one variable at a time if you want a fair test.

items.definitionEn: a result or conclusion that comes out of a study
items.example: The main finding was unexpected and needs a larger trial.

items.definitionEn: so new that it changes a field of study or practice
items.example: A groundbreaking paper forced textbooks to be rewritten.

items.definitionEn: using the newest ideas or technology in a field
items.example: The hospital bought cutting-edge scanning equipment.

items.definitionEn: the best and most modern available at the present time
items.example: The lab has state-of-the-art equipment but too few technicians.

items.definitionEn: a new idea, method or product that is put into use
items.example: Innovation fails if nobody can afford to buy the new tool.

items.definitionEn: a person who is among the first to develop a new idea or method
items.example: She was a pioneer of wireless communication in rural areas.

items.definitionEn: no longer used because something newer and better exists
items.example: Floppy disks are obsolete, yet some factories still depend on them.

items.definitionEn: learning by trying different methods until one works
items.example: Early inventors relied on trial and error more than on theory.

items.definitionEn: a fast, always-on internet connection to a home, school or office
items.example: Rural broadband is still slower than the service in the city.

items.definitionEn: turning data into a code so that only authorised people can read it
items.example: Encryption protects messages if a phone is stolen.

items.definitionEn: a set of rules a computer follows to solve a problem or make a decision
items.example: The recommendation algorithm keeps showing the same type of video.

items.definitionEn: protecting computers, networks and data from attack or unauthorised access
items.example: Cybersecurity is now part of every company’s basic running costs.

items.definitionEn: the trail of data you leave through online activity
items.example: A careless digital footprint can still appear in a job search years later.

items.definitionEn: using remote servers on the internet to store data and run programs
items.example: Cloud computing lets a small firm use huge processing power for a few hours.

items.definitionEn: an organised collection of information that a computer can search quickly
items.example: The hospital database was offline for six hours after the attack.

items.definitionEn: the screens, buttons and menus through which a person controls a program
items.example: A confusing user interface causes errors even when the software is powerful.

items.definitionEn: the amount of data that can be sent over a connection in a given time
items.example: Video lessons collapse when bandwidth is shared by a whole tower block.

items.definitionEn: a cable that carries data as pulses of light
items.example: A fibre-optic cable can bring gigabit speeds to a village if someone pays to lay it.

items.definitionEn: software or hardware that blocks unauthorised traffic in or out of a network
items.example: The school firewall stops some homework sites as well as games.

items.definitionEn: a login method that needs a password plus a second check, such as a code on a phone
items.example: Two-factor authentication stops many stolen passwords from being enough.

items.definitionEn: software designed to damage a device or steal data
items.example: Malware often arrives as an attachment that looks like an invoice.

items.definitionEn: malware that locks files and demands money to unlock them
items.example: Ransomware closed the council’s email for a fortnight.

items.definitionEn: an incident in which private information is copied or seen without permission
items.example: Customers were told to change passwords after the data breach.

items.definitionEn: harmful software that copies itself and can damage files or steal data
items.example: A computer virus spread through a shared USB stick.

items.definitionEn: tricking someone into giving passwords or money through a fake message or site
items.example: The phishing email copied the bank’s logo almost perfectly.

items.definitionEn: the main software that runs a computer and other programs
items.example: The operating system will not support this laptop after next year.

items.definitionEn: a formal language used to write instructions for a computer
items.example: Python is a popular first programming language in schools.

items.definitionEn: the human-readable instructions that make up a program
items.example: Open-source projects publish their source code so others can check it.

items.definitionEn: software whose code can be viewed, changed and shared by others
items.example: Open source tools power much of the internet, often unpaid.

items.definitionEn: a new version of a program that fixes problems or adds features
items.example: A software update closed the security hole within days.

items.definitionEn: a computer that stores data or runs services for other computers
items.example: If the server fails, the whole office loses email.

items.definitionEn: a network that connects devices without cables, usually by radio
items.example: The café wireless network is public, so do not type bank details.

items.definitionEn: a tiny electronic circuit that processes or stores information
items.example: A shortage of microchip supplies delayed car production.

items.definitionEn: a material used to make chips, able to conduct electricity under some conditions
items.example: Taiwan makes a large share of the world’s semiconductor products.

items.definitionEn: keeping files on remote internet servers rather than only on your own device
items.example: Cloud storage is convenient, but you depend on the company’s rules.

items.definitionEn: a period when a computer service is unavailable
items.example: The airline system outage left thousands of passengers in queues.

items.definitionEn: watching video over the internet without downloading the whole file first
items.example: Video streaming uses far more data than sending a message.

items.definitionEn: the set of rules a search engine uses to rank pages
items.example: A change in the search algorithm can destroy a small site’s traffic overnight.

items.definitionEn: a small add-on that changes how a web browser works
items.example: A malicious browser extension can read everything you type.

items.definitionEn: small files a site stores on your device to remember you or track visits
items.example: Rejecting extra cookies still lets the site work; it just tracks you less.

items.definitionEn: the legal rules you accept when you use a digital service
items.example: Nobody reads the user agreement, which is why companies hide fees there.

items.definitionEn: being left out of work or study because of poor access to digital technology
items.example: Digital exclusion grew when lessons moved online and some pupils had no laptop.

items.definitionEn: discarded electronic devices that can leak toxic materials if dumped
items.example: Cheap phones create mountains of e-waste unless they are recycled properly.

items.definitionEn: writing instructions that a computer can follow
items.example: Coding in class is a way to think clearly, not only a path to a tech job.

items.definitionEn: how quickly a computer’s central chip can carry out instructions
items.example: Processor speed matters less for writing essays than for editing film.

items.definitionEn: a short-range wireless link between nearby devices
items.example: A Bluetooth connection can leak audio if you pair in a public place without checking the name.

items.definitionEn: using satellite signals to follow the location of a person or object
items.example: GPS tracking of a phone helps find a stolen bike, but it also raises privacy questions.

items.definitionEn: computer systems that perform tasks that usually need human thinking
items.example: Artificial intelligence can draft a text, but a person must still check the facts.

items.definitionEn: a method in which computers improve at a task by finding patterns in data
items.example: Machine learning is only as fair as the data it is trained on.

items.definitionEn: a computing model loosely inspired by the brain, used in many AI systems
items.example: A neural network can recognise faces, but it cannot explain its guess in human terms.

items.definitionEn: a program that answers questions in written or spoken conversation
items.example: The bank chatbot kept repeating the same three answers.

items.definitionEn: using machines or software to do work with little human control
items.example: Automation in warehouses cut some jobs and created others in maintenance.

items.definitionEn: a car or other vehicle that can drive itself in some or all conditions
items.example: An autonomous vehicle still needs a legal driver in many countries.

items.definitionEn: unfair results from an AI system because of skewed data or design
items.example: AI bias in recruitment tools can copy old discrimination at a larger scale.

items.definitionEn: a video or audio clip that uses AI to make someone appear to say or do things they did not
items.example: A deepfake of a politician can spread faster than a correction.

items.definitionEn: AI methods that let computers work with human speech and writing
items.example: Natural language processing powers translation apps and voice assistants.

items.definitionEn: technology that identifies people by analysing images of their faces
items.example: Facial recognition in shops is sold as security and criticised as mass tracking.

items.definitionEn: making a solid object from a digital design, layer by layer
items.example: 3D printing can produce spare parts that factories no longer stock.

items.definitionEn: a computer-generated world experienced through a headset
items.example: Virtual reality is used in training surgeons as well as in games.

items.definitionEn: technology that adds computer images or information to the real world you see
items.example: Augmented reality can show a visitor the inside of a machine without opening it.

items.definitionEn: electronic devices designed to be worn, such as watches or fitness bands
items.example: Wearable technology collects heart-rate data that insurers would love to buy.

items.definitionEn: a robot built to look or move somewhat like a person
items.example: A humanoid robot makes a good photo, but a wheeled machine may do the job better.

items.definitionEn: workers losing posts because machines or software take over the tasks
items.example: Job displacement from automation hits routine work first, not only factories.

items.definitionEn: a tool or invention that can serve both civilian and harmful military purposes
items.example: A self-driving crash is one debate; dual-use technology in drones is another.

items.definitionEn: software that answers spoken commands on a phone or speaker
items.example: A voice assistant in the kitchen is always listening for its wake word.

items.definitionEn: a still-hypothetical system that could match or exceed human thinking across many tasks
items.example: General AI is a research goal, not a product you can buy this year.

items.definitionEn: changing the genes of an organism in a planned way
items.example: Genetic engineering of crops is tightly regulated in the European Union.

items.definitionEn: a living thing whose DNA has been altered by genetic engineering
items.example: A genetically modified organism must be labelled in many food shops.

items.definitionEn: making a genetically identical copy of an organism or cell
items.example: Cloning a pet is possible in some countries, but it raises welfare questions.

items.definitionEn: the complete set of genetic material of an organism
items.example: Mapping a genome is cheaper now than it was twenty years ago.

items.definitionEn: reading the order of chemical letters in a piece of DNA
items.example: DNA sequencing helped track how the virus changed over time.

items.definitionEn: scientific work on cells that can develop into many types of body tissue
items.example: Stem-cell research is promising and ethically contested at the same time.

items.definitionEn: treatment that tries to cure disease by altering or replacing a gene
items.example: Gene therapy is still rare and extremely expensive.

items.definitionEn: precise techniques for changing DNA at a chosen place
items.example: Gene editing of human embryos is banned or strictly limited in most countries.

items.definitionEn: an informal name for a child whose genes have been chosen or changed before birth
items.example: The phrase designer baby turns a complex ethical debate into a headline.

items.definitionEn: the investigation of space using telescopes, probes and crewed missions
items.example: Space exploration is costly, so countries often share the bill.

items.definitionEn: a vehicle designed to travel in space
items.example: The spacecraft sent photos for twelve years before contact was lost.

items.definitionEn: a large structure in orbit where astronauts live and work
items.example: Experiments on the space station need weightlessness that Earth labs cannot copy.

items.definitionEn: the curved path of an object around a planet or star
items.example: A satellite in low Earth orbit completes a circuit in about ninety minutes.

items.definitionEn: a person trained to travel and work in space
items.example: The astronaut described how Earth looks from the window.

items.definitionEn: an instrument that makes distant objects in space appear closer or clearer
items.example: A space telescope avoids the blurring caused by Earth’s atmosphere.

items.definitionEn: a region in space with gravity so strong that not even light can escape
items.example: A black hole is not an empty hole; it is collapsed mass.

items.definitionEn: the leading scientific explanation of how the universe began from an extremely hot, dense state
items.example: Evidence for the Big Bang includes the leftover microwave glow in the sky.

items.definitionEn: an uncrewed craft sent to study a planet, moon or other object
items.example: The space probe flew past Jupiter and on towards the outer planets.

items.definitionEn: the floating condition in orbit where people and objects appear weightless
items.example: Nausea in zero gravity is a common problem in the first days.

items.definitionEn: the event of sending a rocket from Earth into the sky or space
items.example: A rocket launch can be delayed by high wind at the pad.

items.definitionEn: a small rocky body that orbits the sun, mostly between Mars and Jupiter
items.example: An asteroid the size of a city would be a global disaster if it hit Earth.

items.definitionEn: a project to send a craft or people to Mars
items.example: A crewed Mars mission would last years, not weeks.

items.definitionEn: dead satellites, fragments and other human-made junk in orbit
items.example: Space debris already threatens working satellites.

items.definitionEn: the arrival of a craft on the surface of the Moon
items.example: The first lunar landing in 1969 is still a reference point in debates about cost.

items.definitionEn: a space flight that carries people, not only instruments
items.example: A crewed mission needs life support that a robot does not.

items.definitionEn: coming from outside the Earth or its atmosphere
items.example: No confirmed extraterrestrial life has been found, despite decades of searching.

items.definitionEn: sending a satellite into orbit, usually on a rocket
items.example: A failed satellite launch can cost hundreds of millions.

items.definitionEn: an inability to control time spent on phones, games or social media despite harm
items.example: Screen addiction is discussed in schools as seriously as smoking once was.

items.definitionEn: false or inaccurate information spread on the internet, often without the aim of causing harm
items.example: Online misinformation about vaccines often starts as a misunderstanding, then spreads.

items.definitionEn: false information created or shared on purpose to deceive
items.example: State disinformation during an election is a security issue, not only a media one.

items.definitionEn: an online space where you mainly see views you already agree with
items.example: An online echo chamber makes extreme opinions feel like common sense.

items.definitionEn: personalised results that hide opposing information from you
items.example: A filter bubble can hide a whole news story from your feed.

items.definitionEn: control over how your personal information is collected, stored and shared
items.example: Data privacy laws in Europe give you the right to see what a firm holds on you.

items.definitionEn: close watching of people, often with cameras or digital tracking
items.example: Workplace surveillance of keystrokes is legal in some firms and banned in others.

items.definitionEn: watching large numbers of people, usually by a state or a huge platform
items.example: Mass surveillance is defended as safety and attacked as a threat to democracy.

items.definitionEn: cameras used to watch public or private spaces
items.example: CCTV on every corner has not ended street crime, but it helps after the fact.

items.definitionEn: using someone else’s personal details to steal money or services
items.example: Identity fraud often starts with a leaked password and a reused login.

items.definitionEn: using digital messages or posts to frighten, shame or harass someone
items.example: Cyberbullying follows a pupil home in a way that playground insults did not.

items.definitionEn: a title designed to make you open a page, often by exaggeration
items.example: A clickbait headline trains people to distrust all news.

items.definitionEn: continuing to scroll through bad news even though it makes you feel worse
items.example: Doomscrolling at midnight is a fast way to ruin the next day’s focus.

items.definitionEn: using technology in a way that protects mental health and attention
items.example: Digital wellbeing tools on a phone are easy to switch off, which is the problem.

items.definitionEn: spending so much time on phones or computers that sleep, school or health suffers
items.example: Parents argue about excessive screen use more than about books.

items.definitionEn: options that control who can see your information or activity
items.example: Check privacy settings after every app update; they tend to reset towards sharing.

items.definitionEn: a method in which only the sender and receiver can read a message, not the service in between
items.example: End-to-end encryption protects journalists and criminals, which is why states fight it.

items.definitionEn: legislation that limits how organisations may collect and use personal information
items.example: A data protection law can fine a company that sells addresses without consent.

items.definitionEn: checking claims against reliable evidence before sharing them
items.example: Fact-checking is slower than a rumour, which is why rumours win the first hour.

items.definitionEn: a post or video that is shared by huge numbers of people in a short time
items.example: Viral content is not the same as true content.

items.definitionEn: a person who posts to upset, provoke or derail discussion
items.example: An internet troll wants a reaction; silence is often the only useful reply.

items.definitionEn: product features meant to keep you using an app longer than you intended
items.example: Infinite scroll is a classic example of addictive design.

items.definitionEn: the skill of judging whether an online text is accurate, biased or fake
items.example: Online source evaluation now includes spotting a deepfake, not only sending an email.

items.definitionEn: repeated hostile behaviour towards someone through digital channels
items.example: Online harassment of researchers has made some delete their accounts.

items.definitionEn: recording where a device, and therefore a person, goes
items.example: Location tracking on a shared app can be useful and coercive at the same time.

items.definitionEn: searching large sets of data for patterns, often for profit or prediction
items.example: Data mining of shopping habits is how supermarkets decide what to put on offer.

items.definitionEn: information from the body used to identify a person, such as a face, fingerprint or iris
items.example: Biometric data cannot be changed like a password if it leaks.

items.definitionEn: an electricity network that adjusts supply using digital data
items.example: A smart grid can reduce blackouts during peak evening demand.

items.definitionEn: scientific work on joining atomic nuclei to produce energy
items.example: Fusion research aims to copy the process that powers the sun.

items.definitionEn: a person who creates a new device, process or product
items.example: The inventor spent years on a prototype that nobody wanted to fund.

items.definitionEn: a way of testing ideas through observation, experiment and revision
items.example: The scientific method demands that you drop a theory when the evidence contradicts it.

items.definitionEn: a person whose job is to carry out systematic study in a field
items.example: The researcher refused to publish until another lab had checked the data.

items.definitionEn: a room or building equipped for scientific experiments
items.example: Samples must be labelled before they leave the laboratory.

items.definitionEn: research papers that anyone can read without paying a subscription
items.example: Open access matters in countries that cannot afford journal fees.

items.definitionEn: a machine that uses quantum states to perform certain calculations far faster than ordinary computers
items.example: A practical quantum computer could break some of today’s encryption.

items.definitionEn: everyday objects that connect to the internet and share data
items.example: The Internet of Things turns a fridge into a device that can be hacked.

items.definitionEn: a fifth-generation mobile network designed for higher speed and more devices
items.example: A 5G network can support more sensors in a factory, not only faster phones.

items.definitionEn: an electronic object that connects to a network and can be controlled by software
items.example: A smart device in the bedroom may record audio unless you switch the microphone off.

items.definitionEn: an extremely powerful computer used for complex scientific calculations
items.example: A supercomputer models weather in ways a laptop cannot.

items.definitionEn: an instrument that collects radio waves from space rather than visible light
items.example: A radio telescope can observe objects hidden by dust clouds.

items.definitionEn: a planet that orbits a star other than the Sun
items.example: An exoplanet in the habitable zone still may have no atmosphere we could breathe.

items.definitionEn: the ground centre that directs a space flight
items.example: Mission control delayed the spacewalk because of a fault in the suit.

items.definitionEn: a machine that speeds up particles and smashes them together to study matter
items.example: A particle accelerator is a tool of physics, not a weapon.

items.definitionEn: data that describe other data, such as when a photo was taken or who sent an email
items.example: Metadata can reveal your movements even when the message itself is encrypted.
